Under a lattice translation by \(n\),
\[
c_s(k)\longmapsto e^{ik\cdot n}c_s(k).
\]
Thus a particle–hole expectation value preserves translations only when its creation and annihilation operators have the same momentum. For each \(k\), the resulting \(2\times2\) Hermitian spin-density matrix has four independent components: charge density and three spin components. Arbitrary momentum dependence also includes translation-preserving rotational or nematic order.

\[
\boxed{
\left\langle c^\dagger_\uparrow(k)c_\uparrow(k)\right\rangle+
\left\langle c^\dagger_\downarrow(k)c_\downarrow(k)\right\rangle
\ ;\
\left\langle c^\dagger_\uparrow(k)c_\uparrow(k)\right\rangle-
\left\langle c^\dagger_\downarrow(k)c_\downarrow(k)\right\rangle
\ ;\
\left\langle c^\dagger_\uparrow(k)c_\downarrow(k)\right\rangle+
\left\langle c^\dagger_\downarrow(k)c_\uparrow(k)\right\rangle
\ ;\
-i\!\left(
\left\langle c^\dagger_\uparrow(k)c_\downarrow(k)\right\rangle-
\left\langle c^\dagger_\downarrow(k)c_\uparrow(k)\right\rangle
\right)
}
\]

For a triangular lattice with \(a=1\), the original hexagonal Brillouin zone has circumradius \(4\pi/3\). The \(\sqrt3\times\sqrt3\) periodicity reduces every reciprocal-space dimension by \(1/\sqrt3\), giving circumradius \(4\pi/(3\sqrt3)\). With two corners on the \(k_x\)-axis, the six alternating \(K\) and \(K'\) points are

\[
\boxed{(2.42,\,0.00);\ (1.21,\,2.09);\ (-1.21,\,2.09);\ (-2.42,\,0.00);\ (-1.21,\,-2.09);\ (1.21,\,-2.09)}
\]

The \(\sqrt3\times\sqrt3\) superlattice enlarges the real-space lattice by \(\sqrt3\) and rotates it by \(30^\circ\). Thus the reduced Brillouin zone is scaled by \(1/\sqrt3\) and rotated by \(30^\circ\). Its corner radius is
\[
\frac{1}{\sqrt3}\frac{4\pi}{3a}=\frac{4\pi}{3\sqrt3},
\]
since \(a=1\). Evaluating the six vertices and rounding to two decimal places gives
\[
\boxed{(2.09,\,1.21);\ (0.00,\,2.42);\ (-2.09,\,1.21);\ (-2.09,\,-1.21);\ (0.00,\,-2.42);\ (2.09,\,-1.21)}
\]

Since nearest neighbors lie on opposite sublattices, the staggered sign cancels the fermionic reordering sign in the down-spin hopping. Moreover,
\(n_{i,\uparrow}=m_{i,\uparrow}\) and \(n_{i,\downarrow}=1-m_{i,\downarrow}\). Thus the interaction changes sign, while the centered chemical-potential term becomes a spin-density term:

\[
\boxed{
f_{i,j,\sigma}+g_i
=
-t\!\left(
p_{i,\sigma}^{\dagger}p_{j,\sigma}
+
p_{j,\sigma}^{\dagger}p_{i,\sigma}
\right)
-U\!\left(m_{i,\uparrow}-\frac12\right)
  \left(m_{i,\downarrow}-\frac12\right)
-\mu\!\left(m_{i,\uparrow}-m_{i,\downarrow}\right)
}
\]

Since \(n_{i,\uparrow}=m_{i,\uparrow}\) and \(n_{i,\downarrow}=1-m_{i,\downarrow}\), the interaction changes sign, while the staggered particle–hole transformation preserves the hopping term. Thus

\[
\boxed{
f_{i,j,\sigma}+g_i
=
-t\!\left(p_{i,\sigma}^{\dagger}p_{j,\sigma}
+p_{j,\sigma}^{\dagger}p_{i,\sigma}\right)
-U\!\left(m_{i,\uparrow}-\frac12\right)
\left(m_{i,\downarrow}-\frac12\right)
-\mu\!\left(m_{i,\uparrow}-m_{i,\downarrow}\right)
}
\]

For nearest neighbors \(i,j\), the sublattice signs are opposite. Fermionic anticommutation therefore leaves the hopping term invariant. The densities transform as
\(n_{i,\uparrow}=m_{i,\uparrow}\) and \(n_{i,\downarrow}=1-m_{i,\downarrow}\), reversing the sign of the interaction and converting the chemical-potential coupling into a spin-density coupling.

\[
\boxed{
f_{i,j,\sigma}+g_i
=
-t\!\left(
p_{i,\sigma}^{\dagger}p_{j,\sigma}
+
p_{j,\sigma}^{\dagger}p_{i,\sigma}
\right)
-U\!\left(m_{i,\uparrow}-\frac12\right)
  \left(m_{i,\downarrow}-\frac12\right)
-\mu\left(m_{i,\uparrow}-m_{i,\downarrow}\right)
}
\]

Since \(n_{i,\uparrow}=m_{i,\uparrow}\) and \(n_{i,\downarrow}=1-m_{i,\downarrow}\), the interaction changes sign. The staggered particle–hole transformation leaves the hopping invariant on each A–B bond, while the chemical potential becomes a spin-density term. Thus

\[
\boxed{
f_{i,j,\sigma}+g_i
=
-t\!\left(p_{i,\sigma}^{\dagger}p_{j,\sigma}
+p_{j,\sigma}^{\dagger}p_{i,\sigma}\right)
-U\!\left(m_{i,\uparrow}-\frac12\right)
\!\left(m_{i,\downarrow}-\frac12\right)
-\mu\!\left(m_{i,\uparrow}-m_{i,\downarrow}\right)
}
\]

For nearest neighbors \(i\) and \(j\), the sublattice signs are opposite. Fermionic anticommutation therefore leaves the hopping term invariant. The densities transform as
\[
n_{i,\uparrow}=m_{i,\uparrow},
\qquad
n_{i,\downarrow}=1-m_{i,\downarrow}.
\]
Consequently, the particle-hole-symmetric interaction changes sign, while the chemical-potential term becomes a spin-density term:
\[
U\left(n_{i,\uparrow}-\frac12\right)
 \left(n_{i,\downarrow}-\frac12\right)
=-U\left(m_{i,\uparrow}-\frac12\right)
 \left(m_{i,\downarrow}-\frac12\right),
\]
\[
-\mu\left(n_{i,\uparrow}+n_{i,\downarrow}-1\right)
=-\mu\left(m_{i,\uparrow}-m_{i,\downarrow}\right).
\]

Thus the requested bond-plus-site contribution is
\[
\boxed{
f_{i,j,\sigma}+g_i
=
-t\left(
p^{\dagger}_{i,\sigma}p_{j,\sigma}
+p^{\dagger}_{j,\sigma}p_{i,\sigma}
\right)
-U\left(m_{i,\uparrow}-\frac12\right)
 \left(m_{i,\downarrow}-\frac12\right)
-\mu\left(m_{i,\uparrow}-m_{i,\downarrow}\right)
}
\]

The bipartite transformation separates the fermion into two Majorana sectors. For \(V>0\), the hopping-channel decoupling makes their weights complex conjugates, so the total weight is an absolute square and is nonnegative. For \(V<0\), this conjugate pairing is lost, allowing negative weights and hence a sign problem.

In the Majorana hopping-channel decomposition, repulsive nearest-neighbor interactions between opposite sublattices produce two complex-conjugate Majorana weights. Their product is an absolute square and is therefore nonnegative. For \(V<0\), this conjugacy condition is lost, so negative weights can occur.

At half-filling on a bipartite lattice, the Majorana hopping-channel decomposition yields two Majorana-sector weights related by complex conjugation for \(V>0\). Their product is therefore an absolute square and nonnegative, so there is no sign problem. This positivity does not hold for \(V<0\) in the standard construction, producing a sign problem.

For \(V>0\), the hopping-channel auxiliary field couples identically to the two Majorana components. Bipartiteness and real inter-sublattice hopping make their fermionic weights complex conjugates, so the total weight is an absolute square and is nonnegative.

For \(V<0\), the required hopping-channel decoupling couples the Majorana components with opposite signs, removing this conjugate pairing. The auxiliary-field weight can therefore change sign.

For the even-leg ladder, the strong repulsive interaction \(U=8t\) and transverse hopping \(2t\) produce a spin gap. At \(n=7/8\), doping leaves the charge sector gapless while the spin sector remains gapped, which characterizes a Luther–Emery liquid.

\[
\boxed{\text{(b) Luther--Emery liquid}}
\]

Away from half filling, the total charge mode remains gapless. The two-leg coupling and repulsive interaction gap the spin and relative-charge excitations, leaving one gapless charge mode and a spin gap—the defining structure of a Luther–Emery liquid.

\[
\boxed{\mathrm{(b)\ Luther\text{-}Emery\ liquid}}
\]

The transverse hopping \(2t\) separates the bonding and antibonding bands. At filling \(n=7/8\), only the bonding band remains partially filled. Away from half filling, the repulsive interaction \(U=8t\) leaves both charge and spin excitations gapless, which characterizes a Luttinger liquid rather than a spin-gapped Luther–Emery liquid.

For Stratonovich midpoint discretization with the endpoint measure, the Onsager–Machlup integrand is
\[
\frac14\left(\frac{p+x^3}{x^2}\right)^2
+\frac12x^2\frac{d}{dx}\left(\frac{-x^3}{x^2}\right).
\]
Since \(x\neq0\), this simplifies to

\[
\boxed{\displaystyle \frac{(p+x^3)^2}{4x^4}-\frac{x^2}{2}}
\]

At the midpoint \(x=(x_k+x_{k+1})/2\), the discretized noise is
\[
\eta=\frac{p+x^3}{x^2}.
\]
Its Jacobian, combined with the specified endpoint normalization, contributes \(x^2\) to the continuum action. Hence
\[
S=\int dt\left[\frac{(p+x^3)^2}{4x^4}+x^2\right],\qquad x\ne0.
\]

Therefore, the requested integrand is
\[
\boxed{\displaystyle \frac{(p+x^3)^2}{4x^4}+x^2}
\]
